screens.title: Working with C++ in Blueprints
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we examine how C++ and Blueprints work together inside Unreal Engine and why combining both gives you the best of fast iteration and system-level control. You will learn when to author core systems in C++ and when to expose those systems so designers can extend them visually in Blueprints. We'll highlight the practical specifiers you use to expose functions and properties, and the event patterns you rely on when Blueprints must implement or override C++ logic. The chapter is important because Blueprints are quick for iteration, but C++ is necessary for performance-sensitive systems, low-level engine access, and team scalability. For example, you might implement a robust inventory manager in C++ for memory control, then provide Blueprint events for designers to add item pickup VFX. I will also point out common beginner mistakes, like trying to keep everything in Blueprints when C++ is a better fit. By the end you'll know the specifiers to use and how to design C++ base classes that remain flexible for Blueprint authors. Consider how you would split responsibilities between performance and presentation in your next project.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Working with C++ in Blueprints
Working with C++ in Blueprints
BlueprintCallable, BlueprintImplementableEvent, and BlueprintNativeEvent

Understand how to place core game logic in C++ and expose safe, organized hooks for designers using Blueprints. This chapter shows specifiers, event types, and a hands-on HealthComponent example to bind C++ and Blueprint behavior.

In this lesson
Why C++ and Blueprints together

Practical hybrid workflow and specifiers you will use often.

Coming up

Hands-on

Build a C++ component and bind Blueprint events for visual feedback.

Design-to-Code flow
C++ base systems with Blueprint hooks
Core
C++ for stability & performance
Presentation
Blueprints for visuals & rapid tweaks

Explore Key Topics
Expose functions
UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable) and BlueprintPure let Blueprints call C++ logic safely.
Expose variables

Blueprint events

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives prepare you to design hybrid systems that use C++ for core logic and Blueprints for designer-facing behavior. First, you'll understand the interoperable relationship: C++ is the engine foundation while Blueprints are a visual layer that can call or implement C++ code. Next, you'll identify when C++ is preferable — for high-frequency updates, complex algorithms, or engine-level access — and when Blueprints are fine. Third, you'll learn how to expose C++ functions and variables to Blueprints using UFUNCTION and UPROPERTY specifiers so designers can use those members safely. Finally, you'll implement BlueprintImplementableEvent and BlueprintNativeEvent patterns to allow Blueprint-defined logic to extend or override C++ functionality. Each objective explains a concrete skill: recognizing a performance bottleneck that needs C++, marking a function BlueprintCallable, declaring a BlueprintReadOnly property, or creating an implementable event for VFX. You will finish with a hands-on HealthComponent example that shows these ideas working together. Consider how these skills let teams separate responsibilities between programmers and designers.

screens.title: How C++ and Blueprints relate
screens.narratorSegment: Start by anchoring the relationship: C++ is the engine's foundation, and Blueprints are a visual scripting layer that sits on top. This means C++ provides the classes, memory management patterns, and performance characteristics, while Blueprints make it easy for non-programmers to assemble gameplay, call functions, and react to events. Practically, you design base systems in C++ when you need predictable performance, deterministic memory behavior, or access to low-level engine APIs. For example, a large inventory or AI pathfinder is typically a C++ system because it benefits from careful data layout and optimized loops. Blueprints are ideal for visual responses, level-specific logic, or rapid iteration on gameplay feel. A common misconception is believing Blueprints are slower in all cases; they are slower when used for heavy computation or when the Blueprint graph becomes extremely large, but they are perfectly fine for most gameplay wiring. Another misconception is that exposing every C++ detail to Blueprints is harmless. Overexposing state can lead to tight coupling and accidental modifications. The takeaway is to separate responsibilities: C++ for robust systems and Blueprints for designer-facing extension and presentation. Ask yourself which parts must be stable and which parts should be tweakable by designers.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › How C++ and Blueprints relate
Definition

C++ is the core engine language. Blueprints are a visual layer that calls into, or implements, C++ functionality.

Why it matters
  • Performance and memory control for heavy systems.
  • Designers can iterate on presentation without touching C++.
  • Team workflows improve when responsibilities are split.
Key Takeaway

Choose C++ for stable, high-frequency systems; expose narrow, well-documented hooks to Blueprints.

Concrete example

An inventory manager implemented in C++ for tight memory control. Designers get Blueprint events for pickup VFX and sound so they can tweak presentation per item without touching core logic.

Common mistake

Trying to build every system as Blueprint logic can lead to performance bottlenecks and merge conflicts on larger teams.

C++
Core systems, speed
Blueprints
Presentation, iteration

screens.title: When to prefer C++ over Blueprints
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding when to write C++ is often a balance of needs. Use C++ when performance is critical, such as heavy math loops, frequent updates, or large data processing. C++ also gives access to lower-level engine features or third-party libraries that Blueprints can't reach. Another strong reason is defining core game systems: creating robust base classes for characters, weapons, or inventory in C++ provides stability and predictable APIs for Blueprint subclasses. Finally, in team environments, C++ code can be structured and reviewed in ways that reduce merge conflicts and enforce coding standards. Contrast this with typical Blueprint use-cases: designers iterate quickly, implement visual feedback, and wire event-driven gameplay without recompiling. A common misconception is that C++ always outperforms Blueprints for small gameplay tasks; in reality, the overhead of calling into C++ from Blueprint or vice versa is negligible for occasional events, and keeping simple behavior in Blueprints speeds iteration. When in doubt, profile: move hotspots to C++ and keep presentation in Blueprints. The question to ask is: is the code a stability boundary or a creative surface? When to prefer C++ over Blueprints means prefer c++ for hotspots, low-level access, and stable base classes; use blueprints for designer iteration and presentation.. In practical terms, performance, access, and team workflows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › When to prefer C++ over Blueprints
C++ — Use when
  • Performance is paramount: heavy math, large loops, fixed-timestep updates.
  • Access to low-level engine APIs or third-party libraries is required.
  • Defining core base classes for consistency across the project.
  • Large teams need stricter version control and code review workflows.
Example: pathfinding, physics helpers, or inventory back ends.
Blueprints — Use when
  • Rapid iteration on gameplay feel or visual responses.
  • Designer-driven tuning without a C++ compile step.
  • Small logic and event wiring with low-frequency calls.
Misconception check

Not every function belongs in C++; small gameplay wiring in Blueprints is fine and often faster for iteration.

Profile
Measure before porting to C++.
Boundaries
Make a clear API for Blueprint use.
Team
Centralize complex logic in C++ for reviewability.

screens.title: Exposing functions: UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
screens.narratorSegment: Exposing a C++ function to Blueprint is done with a UFUNCTION specifier, most commonly BlueprintCallable or BlueprintPure. BlueprintCallable makes the function available as a node in Blueprint graphs so designers can trigger it at runtime. BlueprintPure describes a function that does not modify state and can be used as a pure node that returns a value. A concrete example from the chapter shows a character class exposing MyCustomCPlusPlusFunction as BlueprintCallable and GetCurrentHealth as BlueprintCallable plus BlueprintPure. After you add the declaration in the header, implement the body in the source file and compile. One common mistake is forgetting to compile the project after editing headers; the Blueprint editor will not show the new node until you compile. Another pitfall is marking functions BlueprintCallable when they change internal state unexpectedly; prefer BlueprintPure for read-only queries. For designers, the availability of these nodes offers a clear A P I surface. The takeaway is to expose only the functions designers need and document the behavior so Blueprint authors know whether a node changes state or is read-only. How would you choose between a callable or a pure node for a health query?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Expose Functions
Concept

UFUNCTION with BlueprintCallable exposes actions to Blueprint graphs. BlueprintPure marks read-only queries.

  • Declare in header with the proper specifier and Category for organization.
  • Implement in the .cpp file and compile the project.
  • Document whether the function mutates state to guide designers.
Pro tip

Group Blueprint-exposed functions into coherent categories for editor discoverability.

Code example
// MyCharacter.h
UCLASS()
class MYGAME_API AMyCharacter : public ACharacter
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Character Actions")
    void MyCustomCPlusPlusFunction();

    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, BlueprintPure, Category = "Character Info")
    float GetCurrentHealth() const;
};

// MyCharacter.cpp
void AMyCharacter::MyCustomCPlusPlusFunction()
{
    // C++ logic here
    UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("MyCustomCPlusPlusFunction called from Blueprint!"));
}

float AMyCharacter::GetCurrentHealth() const
{
    return HealthComponent->GetCurrentHealth();
}
Remember to compile so Blueprint nodes appear. Use Category to organize nodes in the editor.

screens.title: Exposing variables: UPROPERTY(BlueprintReadWrite / BlueprintReadOnly)
screens.narratorSegment: UPROPERTY tags control what Blueprints can see and change. Use BlueprintReadWrite for designer-editable runtime properties when a Blueprint must both read and set a value. Use BlueprintReadOnly when you want Blueprints to observe state without modifying it, which is helpful to prevent unintended side effects. The chapter example shows MaxHealth marked EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite so designers can tune maximum health in the editor and change it at runtime; CurrentHealth is VisibleAnywhere and BlueprintReadOnly so Blueprints can display it but not directly assign it. Remember that EditAnywhere and VisibleAnywhere control editor visibility and whether a property can be changed from the details panel. A practical misconception is making everything ReadWrite — that invites accidental bugs. Instead, expose only what is necessary and provide BlueprintCallable functions for controlled changes. When exposing rich types or arrays, consider how replication and serialization behave and document expected usage. After changing a header, compile and verify the property appears correctly in the Blueprint details panel. The takeaway: expose state intentionally and prefer functions to change critical internal variables. Exposing variables: UPROPERTY(BlueprintReadWrite / BlueprintReadOnly) means use readonly for observable state, readwrite for designer-editable variables, and functions for controlled mutation.. In practical terms, control designer access to c++ state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Expose Variables
Principles
  • BlueprintReadWrite: allow read and write from Blueprints.
  • BlueprintReadOnly: allow read-only access to state.
  • EditAnywhere / VisibleAnywhere control editor visibility and editability.
Misconception

Marking everything ReadWrite leads to accidental coupling; prefer functions to mutate sensitive state.

Key Takeaway

Expose minimal state. Use properties for values, functions for controlled changes.

Code example
// MyCharacter.h
UCLASS()
class MYGAME_API AMyCharacter : public ACharacter
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Character Stats")
    float MaxHealth;

    UPROPERTY(VisibleAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Character State")
    bool bIsDead;
};
EditAnywhere allows designers to set defaults in the editor. VisibleAnywhere shows runtime values without making them editable.

screens.title: Editor categories, compile, and verify
screens.narratorSegment: When you add UFUNCTION or UPROPERTY changes, the workflow is simple but must be followed precisely. First, declare the specifier and Category in the header. Category organizes nodes and properties in the Blueprint editor so designers can find them. Second, implement the function or initialize the property in the. cpp file. Third, compile your C++ project — either in your IDE or using the Compile button in the Unreal Editor. The editor will not surface new Blueprint-callable functions or properties until compilation completes. Fourth, open or refresh the Blueprint that will use the A P I and check the details panel and context menus. A useful checklist: add Category for discoverability, prefer BlueprintPure for queries, mark editability with EditAnywhere when a property should be editable in defaults, and always test the new node in a simple Blueprint graph. Common mistakes include forgetting Generated. h or syntax errors that block compilation; these errors will stop the reflection system from registering your types. If compilation fails, read the output log carefully — Unreal's errors are usually descriptive. The final step is iteration: adjust specifiers or signatures and repeat until the designer experience is clear and safe.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Compile & Verify
Step-by-step
  1. Declare UFUNCTION / UPROPERTY with Category and desired specifiers in the header.
  2. Implement behavior in the .cpp file and initialize properties where needed.
  3. Compile the C++ project in your IDE or use the editor Compile button.
  4. Refresh or re-open Blueprints and check the context menu and details panel.
  5. Test nodes and bindings, iterate on signatures and access control.
Editor tip
Use Category to group functions logically for designers.
Error handling
Read the compile output log to find missing includes or syntax errors.
Check your understanding

After compiling, does the function show in the Blueprint context menu and is the property visible in the details panel?

screens.title: BlueprintImplementableEvent
screens.narratorSegment: BlueprintImplementableEvent declares a function in C++ with no native implementation that Blueprints implement. It is ideal when C++ needs a hook to trigger designer-defined behavior, such as playing a weapon firing VFX or audio. The C++ code calls the event function and relies on the Blueprint to supply the response. For example, a C++ weapon class can declare OnWeaponFired as BlueprintImplementableEvent; the Fire method performs raycast and ammo reduction and then calls OnWeaponFired so each Blueprint weapon can implement different visual effects. A common misconception is thinking the C++ class can provide a fallback — it cannot. If no Blueprint implements the event, nothing happens when it is called. Use ImplementableEvent for required designer hooks where C++ does not need a default action. When you want a fallback, choose BlueprintNativeEvent instead. The takeaway is to use ImplementableEvent to separate engine logic from presentation: C++ handles deterministic systems, while Blueprints provide flexible presentation that is implemented per subclass. What visual or audio responses in your project could be implemented this way? BlueprintImplementableEvent means use blueprintimplementableevent to declare c++ hooks that blueprints implement for presentation or variation.. In practical terms, declare hooks that blueprints must implement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › BlueprintImplementableEvent
What it is

A function declared in C++ with no native implementation. Blueprints implement it as an Event node.

When to use
  • When C++ triggers events that are presentation-specific.
  • When each Blueprint subclass should supply unique visual behavior.
Misconception: Implementable events do not provide a C++ fallback.
Code & example
// MyWeapon.h
UCLASS()
class MYGAME_API AMyWeapon : public AActor
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    UFUNCTION(BlueprintImplementableEvent, Category = "Weapon")
    void OnWeaponFired(); // Blueprint implements this

    void Fire(); // C++ calls OnWeaponFired
};

// MyWeapon.cpp
void AMyWeapon::Fire()
{
    // C++ logic for firing (raycast, ammo reduction)
    OnWeaponFired(); // Call the Blueprint-implemented event
}
In Blueprint subclass: implement Event OnWeaponFired and add particle or sound nodes.

screens.title: BlueprintNativeEvent and Parent Call
screens.narratorSegment: BlueprintNativeEvent declares a function that can have a default C++ implementation and can be overridden by Blueprints. The pattern requires a native implementation method with the _Implementation suffix. When C++ calls the event, Unreal dispatches to the Blueprint override if present; otherwise it calls the C++ implementation. This is powerful when you want baseline behavior and allow designers to extend or replace it. For example, a door actor can provide OpenDoor_Implementation that rotates the door by default. A Blueprint can override OpenDoor to add particle effects or different timing. If the Blueprint wants to run the default logic in addition to its override, it should call Parent Call: OpenDoor at the start of its event graph. A common misconception is thinking overriding always runs both implementations — it does not. If the Blueprint override does not include Parent Call, the C++ default is skipped entirely. Decide whether your default should be authoritative or merely a convenience for designers. The takeaway: use native events when a sensible default behavior exists but designers may need to customize it. BlueprintNativeEvent and Parent Call means use blueprintnativeevent for a c++ default implementation that blueprints can override and optionally call via parent call.. In practical terms, provide defaults and let blueprints override. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › BlueprintNativeEvent
Pattern

Declare UFUNCTION(BlueprintNativeEvent) in the header and provide _Implementation in the .cpp for the default behavior.

Parent Call

Blueprint overrides can call the parent C++ implementation explicitly using Parent Call if they want both behaviors.

Misconception: overriding always runs C++ default — it runs only if the Blueprint calls the parent explicitly.
Code example
// MyDoor.h
UCLASS()
class MYGAME_API AMyDoor : public AActor
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    UFUNCTION(BlueprintNativeEvent, Category = "Door")
    void OpenDoor();

    // The _Implementation method defines the C++ default
    void OpenDoor_Implementation();
};

// MyDoor.cpp
void AMyDoor::OpenDoor_Implementation()
{
    UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("C++ Default OpenDoor called!"));
    // Default rotation logic
}
In Blueprint override: add Parent Call to invoke C++ default, or omit to replace it entirely.

screens.title: Event Dispatchers and binding patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Event dispatchers are a powerful C++ to Blueprint mechanism for broadcasting changes. In C++ you can declare a dynamic multicast delegate type, add a UPROPERTY with BlueprintAssignable, and then broadcast from C++. Blueprints can bind to these dispatchers and react when events occur. The chapter's HealthComponent uses DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE variants and provides OnHealthChanged and OnDamageTaken dispatchers. This allows any Blueprint owning the component to add event handlers without needing to override or subclass the component. A common advantage is loose coupling: the component broadcasts changes and listeners decide how to respond. A common mistake is relying on dispatchers for one-to-one communication when a direct function call would be clearer. Also, dynamic multicast delegates are suitable for Blueprint binding but have a performance cost compared with raw function calls, so prefer them for presentation or low-frequency events. The takeaway is to use dispatchers to notify Blueprints about state changes while keeping C++ logic focused on deterministic state updates. How might you use an OnItemPickedUp dispatcher in an inventory system to trigger UI and sound? content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Event Dispatchers
Pattern

Declare dynamic multicast delegates in C++, mark them BlueprintAssignable, and broadcast from C++ when state changes occur.

When to use
  • To notify UI, VFX, or other Blueprint systems of state changes.
  • For decoupled systems where listeners subscribe at runtime.
Performance note: dynamic delegates are convenient for Blueprint binding but consider direct calls for hot paths.
HealthComponent snippet
DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_TwoParams(FOnHealthChanged, float, CurrentHealth, float, MaxHealth);
DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam(FOnTakeDamage, float, DamageAmount);

UPROPERTY(BlueprintAssignable, Category = "Health")
FOnHealthChanged OnHealthChanged;

UPROPERTY(BlueprintAssignable, Category = "Health")
FOnTakeDamage OnDamageTaken;

// Broadcast when health changes
OnHealthChanged.Broadcast(CurrentHealth, MaxHealth);
In Blueprint: bind to OnHealthChanged and update UI or play sound when broadcasted.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › HealthComponent Example
HealthComponent.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "Components/ActorComponent.h"
#include "HealthComponent.generated.h"

DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_TwoParams(FOnHealthChanged, float, CurrentHealth, float, MaxHealth);
DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam(FOnTakeDamage, float, DamageAmount);

UCLASS( ClassGroup=(Custom), meta=(BlueprintSpawnableComponent) )
class MYGAME_API UHealthComponent : public UActorComponent
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    UHealthComponent();

protected:
    virtual void BeginPlay() override;

public:
    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Health")
    float MaxHealth;

    UPROPERTY(VisibleAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Health")
    float CurrentHealth;

    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Health")
    void TakeDamage(float DamageAmount);

    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Health")
    void Heal(float HealAmount);

    UFUNCTION(BlueprintImplementableEvent, Category = "Health")
    void OnHealthDepleted();

    UPROPERTY(BlueprintAssignable, Category = "Health")
    FOnHealthChanged OnHealthChanged;

    UPROPERTY(BlueprintAssignable, Category = "Health")
    FOnTakeDamage OnDamageTaken;
};
HealthComponent.cpp
#include "HealthComponent.h"

UHealthComponent::UHealthComponent()
{
    PrimaryComponentTick.bCanEverTick = false;
    MaxHealth = 100.0f;
    CurrentHealth = MaxHealth;
}

void UHealthComponent::BeginPlay()
{
    Super::BeginPlay();
    CurrentHealth = MaxHealth;
    OnHealthChanged.Broadcast(CurrentHealth, MaxHealth);
}

void UHealthComponent::TakeDamage(float DamageAmount)
{
    if (DamageAmount <= 0.0f || CurrentHealth <= 0.0f) return;

    CurrentHealth -= DamageAmount;
    CurrentHealth = FMath::Max(0.0f, CurrentHealth);

    UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Took %f damage. Current Health: %f"), DamageAmount, CurrentHealth);

    OnDamageTaken.Broadcast(DamageAmount);
    OnHealthChanged.Broadcast(CurrentHealth, MaxHealth);

    if (CurrentHealth <= 0.0f)
    {
        OnHealthDepleted();
    }
}

void UHealthComponent::Heal(float HealAmount)
{
    if (HealAmount <= 0.0f || CurrentHealth >= MaxHealth) return;

    CurrentHealth += HealAmount;
    CurrentHealth = FMath::Min(MaxHealth, CurrentHealth);

    UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Healed %f. Current Health: %f"), HealAmount, CurrentHealth);
    OnHealthChanged.Broadcast(CurrentHealth, MaxHealth);
}
Hands-on steps
Create the C++ component, compile, add it to a Blueprint character, bind OnHealthChanged and OnDamageTaken in the Blueprint, and implement OnHealthDepleted to play VFX or print a string.

screens.title: Debugging and common compilation errors
screens.narratorSegment: Working with Unreal's reflection system introduces a few recurring pitfalls. First, missing or misordered includes or forgetting to include the generated header can cause compilation failures. Ensure Generated. h is included at the top of your header file. Second, syntax errors in headers prevent UnrealHeaderTool from generating reflection metadata, which stops Blueprint exposure. Always fix header errors first. Third, incorrect specifier usage — for example attempting to BlueprintImplementableEvent with an implementation defined in C++ — causes design confusion. BlueprintImplementableEvent provides no C++ fallback; using NativeEvent is the correct choice when a default is needed. Fourth, not recompiling after header edits is a common oversight; the editor does not automatically pick up new Blueprint nodes until you compile. Use the IDE output and the editor log to find the root cause; Unreal's messages point to the file and line number that failed processing. A useful debugging pattern is to simplify the failing header to the smallest example that still fails, then reintroduce pieces. The takeaway: treat the reflection step as a strict gate — fix header and reflection errors before expecting Blueprint exposure.

Warning › Debugging & Compilation
Common issues
  • Missing includes or Generated.h in the header prevents reflection processing.
  • Syntax errors in headers block UnrealHeaderTool and stop code generation.
  • Incorrect specifier choice confuses intended behavior between implementable and native events.
  • Forgetting to compile means Blueprints won't see new nodes or properties.
Debug tip
Use the compiler and editor logs; they usually point to the problematic file.
Repair flow
Reduce the header to minimal content, recompile, then add declarations back incrementally.
Try this

If a Blueprint node is missing, recompile and check the header for syntax or reflection macro issues before changing Blueprints.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we examine how C++ and Blueprints work together inside Unreal Engine and why combining both gives you the best of fast iteration and system-level control. You will learn when to author core systems in C++ and when to expose those systems so designers can extend them visually in Blueprints. We'll highlight the practical specifiers you use to expose functions and properties, and the event patterns you rely on when Blueprints must implement or override C++ logic. The chapter is important because Blueprints are quick for iteration, but C++ is necessary for performance-sensitive systems, low-level engine access, and team scalability. For example, you might implement a robust inventory manager in C++ for memory control, then provide Blueprint events for designers to add item pickup VFX. I will also point out common beginner mistakes, like trying to keep everything in Blueprints when C++ is a better fit. By the end you'll know the specifiers to use and how to design C++ base classes that remain flexible for Blueprint authors. Consider how you would split responsibilities between performance and presentation in your next project.

These objectives prepare you to design hybrid systems that use C++ for core logic and Blueprints for designer-facing behavior. First, you'll understand the interoperable relationship: C++ is the engine foundation while Blueprints are a visual layer that can call or implement C++ code. Next, you'll identify when C++ is preferable — for high-frequency updates, complex algorithms, or engine-level access — and when Blueprints are fine. Third, you'll learn how to expose C++ functions and variables to Blueprints using UFUNCTION and UPROPERTY specifiers so designers can use those members safely. Finally, you'll implement BlueprintImplementableEvent and BlueprintNativeEvent patterns to allow Blueprint-defined logic to extend or override C++ functionality. Each objective explains a concrete skill: recognizing a performance bottleneck that needs C++, marking a function BlueprintCallable, declaring a BlueprintReadOnly property, or creating an implementable event for VFX. You will finish with a hands-on HealthComponent example that shows these ideas working together. Consider how these skills let teams separate responsibilities between programmers and designers.

This second objectives slide emphasizes the practical outcomes you will deliver. You will be able to declare a UFUNCTION as BlueprintCallable so designers can call C++ behavior from a Blueprint graph. You'll choose BlueprintReadWrite or BlueprintReadOnly on UPROPERTY fields to control editing and runtime access. You'll create BlueprintImplementableEvent hooks for designers to implement visual or audio feedback without changing C++ code. And you'll learn to use BlueprintNativeEvent when you want a C++ default implementation but still allow Blueprint overrides. Each objective maps to a concrete action: add a specifier to a header file, compile the module, and wire events in a Blueprint subclass. The hands-on HealthComponent at the end stitches these actions together, showing how OnHealthDepleted is declared in C++ and implemented in Blueprint with print strings or VFX. Think about how these skills let teams separate code stability from creative iteration, and how the right specifier prevents accidental state mutation or missing implementations.

Start by anchoring the relationship: C++ is the engine's foundation, and Blueprints are a visual scripting layer that sits on top. This means C++ provides the classes, memory management patterns, and performance characteristics, while Blueprints make it easy for non-programmers to assemble gameplay, call functions, and react to events. Practically, you design base systems in C++ when you need predictable performance, deterministic memory behavior, or access to low-level engine APIs. For example, a large inventory or AI pathfinder is typically a C++ system because it benefits from careful data layout and optimized loops. Blueprints are ideal for visual responses, level-specific logic, or rapid iteration on gameplay feel. A common misconception is believing Blueprints are slower in all cases; they are slower when used for heavy computation or when the Blueprint graph becomes extremely large, but they are perfectly fine for most gameplay wiring. Another misconception is that exposing every C++ detail to Blueprints is harmless. Overexposing state can lead to tight coupling and accidental modifications. The takeaway is to separate responsibilities: C++ for robust systems and Blueprints for designer-facing extension and presentation. Ask yourself which parts must be stable and which parts should be tweakable by designers.

Deciding when to write C++ is often a balance of needs. Use C++ when performance is critical, such as heavy math loops, frequent updates, or large data processing. C++ also gives access to lower-level engine features or third-party libraries that Blueprints can't reach. Another strong reason is defining core game systems: creating robust base classes for characters, weapons, or inventory in C++ provides stability and predictable APIs for Blueprint subclasses. Finally, in team environments, C++ code can be structured and reviewed in ways that reduce merge conflicts and enforce coding standards. Contrast this with typical Blueprint use-cases: designers iterate quickly, implement visual feedback, and wire event-driven gameplay without recompiling. A common misconception is that C++ always outperforms Blueprints for small gameplay tasks; in reality, the overhead of calling into C++ from Blueprint or vice versa is negligible for occasional events, and keeping simple behavior in Blueprints speeds iteration. When in doubt, profile: move hotspots to C++ and keep presentation in Blueprints. The question to ask is: is the code a stability boundary or a creative surface? When to prefer C++ over Blueprints means prefer c++ for hotspots, low-level access, and stable base classes; use blueprints for designer iteration and presentation.. In practical terms, performance, access, and team workflows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Exposing a C++ function to Blueprint is done with a UFUNCTION specifier, most commonly BlueprintCallable or BlueprintPure. BlueprintCallable makes the function available as a node in Blueprint graphs so designers can trigger it at runtime. BlueprintPure describes a function that does not modify state and can be used as a pure node that returns a value. A concrete example from the chapter shows a character class exposing MyCustomCPlusPlusFunction as BlueprintCallable and GetCurrentHealth as BlueprintCallable plus BlueprintPure. After you add the declaration in the header, implement the body in the source file and compile. One common mistake is forgetting to compile the project after editing headers; the Blueprint editor will not show the new node until you compile. Another pitfall is marking functions BlueprintCallable when they change internal state unexpectedly; prefer BlueprintPure for read-only queries. For designers, the availability of these nodes offers a clear A P I surface. The takeaway is to expose only the functions designers need and document the behavior so Blueprint authors know whether a node changes state or is read-only. How would you choose between a callable or a pure node for a health query?

UPROPERTY tags control what Blueprints can see and change. Use BlueprintReadWrite for designer-editable runtime properties when a Blueprint must both read and set a value. Use BlueprintReadOnly when you want Blueprints to observe state without modifying it, which is helpful to prevent unintended side effects. The chapter example shows MaxHealth marked EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite so designers can tune maximum health in the editor and change it at runtime; CurrentHealth is VisibleAnywhere and BlueprintReadOnly so Blueprints can display it but not directly assign it. Remember that EditAnywhere and VisibleAnywhere control editor visibility and whether a property can be changed from the details panel. A practical misconception is making everything ReadWrite — that invites accidental bugs. Instead, expose only what is necessary and provide BlueprintCallable functions for controlled changes. When exposing rich types or arrays, consider how replication and serialization behave and document expected usage. After changing a header, compile and verify the property appears correctly in the Blueprint details panel. The takeaway: expose state intentionally and prefer functions to change critical internal variables. Exposing variables: UPROPERTY(BlueprintReadWrite / BlueprintReadOnly) means use readonly for observable state, readwrite for designer-editable variables, and functions for controlled mutation.. In practical terms, control designer access to c++ state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you add UFUNCTION or UPROPERTY changes, the workflow is simple but must be followed precisely. First, declare the specifier and Category in the header. Category organizes nodes and properties in the Blueprint editor so designers can find them. Second, implement the function or initialize the property in the. cpp file. Third, compile your C++ project — either in your IDE or using the Compile button in the Unreal Editor. The editor will not surface new Blueprint-callable functions or properties until compilation completes. BlueprintImplementableEvent declares a function in C++ with no native implementation that Blueprints implement. It is ideal when C++ needs a hook to trigger designer-defined behavior, such as playing a weapon firing VFX or audio. The C++ code calls the event function and relies on the Blueprint to supply the response. For example, a C++ weapon class can declare OnWeaponFired as BlueprintImplementableEvent; the Fire method performs raycast and ammo reduction and then calls OnWeaponFired so each Blueprint weapon can implement different visual effects. A common misconception is thinking the C++ class can provide a fallback — it cannot. If no Blueprint implements the event, nothing happens when it is called. Use ImplementableEvent for required designer hooks where C++ does not need a default action. When you want a fallback, choose BlueprintNativeEvent instead. The takeaway is to use ImplementableEvent to separate engine logic from presentation: C++ handles deterministic systems, while Blueprints provide flexible presentation that is implemented per subclass. BlueprintNativeEvent declares a function that can have a default C++ implementation and can be overridden by Blueprints. The pattern requires a native implementation method with the _Implementation suffix. When C++ calls the event, Unreal dispatches to the Blueprint override if present; otherwise it calls the C++ implementation. This is powerful when you want baseline behavior and allow designers to extend or replace it. For example, a door actor can provide OpenDoor_Implementation that rotates the door by default. A Blueprint can override OpenDoor to add particle effects or different timing. If the Blueprint wants to run the default logic in addition to its override, it should call Parent Call: OpenDoor at the start of its event graph. A common misconception is thinking overriding always runs both implementations — it does not. If the Blueprint override does not include Parent Call, the C++ default is skipped entirely. Decide whether your default should be authoritative or merely a convenience for designers. The takeaway: use native events when a sensible default behavior exists but designers may need to customize it. Working with Unreal's reflection system introduces a few recurring pitfalls. First, missing or misordered includes or forgetting to include the generated header can cause compilation failures. Ensure Generated. h is included at the top of your header file. Second, syntax errors in headers prevent UnrealHeaderTool from generating reflection metadata, which stops Blueprint exposure. Always fix header errors first. Third, incorrect specifier usage — for example attempting to BlueprintImplementableEvent with an implementation defined in C++ — causes design confusion. BlueprintImplementableEvent provides no C++ fallback; using NativeEvent is the correct choice when a default is needed. Fourth, not recompiling after header edits is a common oversight; the editor does not automatically pick up new Blueprint nodes until you compile. Use the IDE output and the editor log to find the root cause; Unreal's messages point to the file and line number that failed processing. A useful debugging pattern is to simplify the failing header to the smallest example that still fails, then reintroduce pieces. The takeaway: treat the reflection step as a strict gate — fix header and reflection errors before expecting Blueprint exposure.

Let's recap the essential terms and how you will use them. BlueprintCallable exposes C++ functions as Blueprint nodes so designers can call engine logic. BlueprintReadWrite and BlueprintReadOnly control whether Blueprints may modify or only read C++ properties, which is crucial for safe designer workflows. BlueprintImplementableEvent declares a hook that Blueprints must implement for presentation logic; it has no C++ fallback. Use BlueprintNativeEvent when you want a C++ default that Blueprints can override, and remember that Blueprint overrides skip the C++ default unless the Blueprint uses Parent Call. Finally, UFUNCTION and UPROPERTY are the macros that make the reflection and exposure possible. Each of these concepts maps directly to a design decision: whether to provide a default, whether to allow modification, and how designers will interact with your C++ classes.
